# **Verification and Validation Protocols for Finite Volume Method Simulators in Relativistic and Newtonian Magnetohydrodynamics**

## **Introduction to Computational Trust and the Verification Framework**

The maturation of computational physics requires establishing rigorous, quantifiable confidence in numerical simulations through formalized verification and validation (V\&V) protocols. In the domain of fluid dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics (MHD)—particularly when extending into the extreme, non-linear regimes of General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD)—the complexity of the partial differential equations demands an exhaustive approach to software quality assurance.1 Verification assesses whether the underlying mathematical model is solved correctly, isolating software bugs, spatial and temporal discretization errors, and algorithmic consistency.4 Validation, conversely, determines whether the chosen mathematical model accurately represents the physical reality by comparing simulation outputs against high-fidelity experimental measurements or observational data.5 Developers of computer codes, the analysts who utilize them, and the decision-makers who rely upon their outputs face a critical mandate to rigorously assess the credibility of their simulations.7  
The development of numerical software, such as the FiniteVolumeMethod.jl package written in the Julia programming language, necessitates a highly structured sequence of code verification tests. Because this software is uniquely designed to handle a hierarchy of physical models—ranging from fully relativistic GRMHD down to the classical Navier-Stokes limit—the verification suite must systematically probe the continuous reduction of these mathematical frameworks.8 The codebase features unstructured and curvilinear mesh capabilities, multiple approximate Riemann solvers (including HLL and HLLD), flux limiters for high-resolution shock-capturing (HRSC), and a staggered grid implementation for Constrained Transport. Furthermore, the software integrates with the broader SciML ecosystem via sciml\_bridge.jl, casting assembled spatial discretizations into standard ordinary differential equation (ODE) problems. To elevate this codebase to the standard of a polished, production-ready software product, it must be subjected to industry-standard V\&V protocols, notably the guidelines established by the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) V\&V 20-2009 standards and the National Agency for Finite Element Methods and Standards (NAFEMS).2  
This report provides an exhaustive architecture for the verification of FiniteVolumeMethod.jl. It defines the theoretical foundation of the underlying physics, details the exact configuration of manufactured and analytical benchmark solutions, and establishes the quantitative metrics required to prove asymptotic convergence and mathematical correctness across the entire hierarchy of supported physical models.

## **Theoretical Foundation and the Mathematical Reduction Hierarchy**

The governing equations implemented within the software are formulated using the 3+1 Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) decomposition of spacetime, coupled with the Valencia formulation of GRMHD.8 This formulation casts the equations of baryon number conservation and energy-momentum conservation into a strongly hyperbolic, flux-conservative form, which is absolutely critical for the application of Finite Volume Methods (FVM) and Godunov-type shock-capturing schemes.11 The Lax-Wendroff theorem guarantees that if a consistent numerical method written in a flux-conservative form converges, it converges to a weak solution of the conservation law, ensuring the correct propagation of shocks and discontinuities.13  
The spacetime metric line element in the 3+1 formalism is defined to foliate four-dimensional spacetime into three-dimensional spatial hypersurfaces evolving in coordinate time:  
![][image1]  
Here, ![][image2] is the lapse function which dictates the rate at which proper time elapses relative to coordinate time, ![][image3] is the shift vector which describes the movement of the spatial coordinates from one hypersurface to the next, and ![][image4] is the spatial metric measuring distances within the 3D spatial slice.8 The volume factor ![][image5] is essential for calculating proper volumes in curved spacetime.8 The Valencia formulation evolves a vector of conserved variables ![][image6], calculating fluxes ![][image7] across cell interfaces, and applying geometric source terms ![][image8].8 The system is expressed as:  
![][image9]  
The conserved variables ![][image10] correspond to the rest-mass density, the momentum density, and the energy density measured by an Eulerian observer moving along the normal vector to the spatial hypersurface.8 The stress-energy tensor ![][image11] encapsulates the fluid and electromagnetic properties:  
![][image12]  
The source vector ![][image8] contains the contractions of the stress-energy tensor with the derivatives of the metric.8 Physically, these geometric source terms represent the exchange of momentum and energy between the fluid and the gravitational field, effectively modeling gravitational acceleration and the work done by the spacetime curvature.8 For instance, the momentum source term incorporates ![][image13], which acts analogously to a gravitational potential gradient accelerating the fluid into regions of deeper gravitational potential.8

### **Asymptotic Reduction to Simpler Physics**

A foundational pillar of verifying a GRMHD code is proving that it correctly reduces to simpler physical regimes when appropriate limits are applied.8 The FiniteVolumeMethod.jl package defines various equation models within its models.jl architecture (e.g., Diffusion1D, Advection2D, AdvectionDiffusion3D).15 The generalized GRMHD solver must perfectly recover these discrete behaviors without introducing spurious numerical artifacts.  
The first critical reduction is to the Special Relativistic MHD (SRMHD) limit. This occurs when spacetime is strictly flat (Minkowski space). In this limit, the lapse function ![][image14], the shift vector ![][image15], and the spatial metric determinant ![][image16].8 Because the metric is constant across the entire spatial domain, all metric derivatives vanish. Consequently, the geometric source terms ![][image8] identically become zero.8 Furthermore, the distinction between the Eulerian observer frame and the coordinate frame disappears.8 Verification of this limit requires initiating the GRMHD solver in a flat Minkowski background and ensuring that the source term computation routines yield machine-zero, preventing unphysical accelerations in flat space.  
The second reduction is to the Newtonian MHD limit. This is recovered under conditions of weak gravity (![][image17]), non-relativistic fluid velocities (![][image18]), and rest-mass dominance, where internal energy and magnetic pressure are negligible compared to the rest-mass energy (![][image19]).8 Under these constraints, the conserved rest-mass density ![][image20] reduces directly to the classical density ![][image21], and the momentum density ![][image22] approximates to ![][image23].8 The Newtonian energy density is recovered by subtracting the rest-mass density from the conserved energy density, yielding ![][image24].8 The verification of this limit is vital for establishing that the recovery of primitive variables (via Newton-Raphson iteration in the Con2Prim routines) remains stable and accurate when Lorentz factors approach unity (![][image25]) and relativistic enthalpies approximate to the rest mass.8  
The third reduction encompasses the Navier-Stokes and viscous limits. While the standard GRMHD equations describe an ideal, inviscid fluid, physical realism often requires modeling dissipation.8 Extending relativistic hydrodynamics to include viscosity traditionally faced severe challenges regarding causality and stability, leading to the development of Israel-Stewart-type theories.17 The Israel-Stewart formulation treats the viscous stress tensor as a highly dynamic variable governed by a specific relaxation time ![][image26] to maintain subluminal signal propagation.8 Verification of the viscous limit requires demonstrating that by taking the relaxation time to zero (![][image27]), the system seamlessly recovers the structure of the relativistic Navier-Stokes equations.8 In the further limit where ![][image18], the complex relativistic fluid shear tensor must reduce to the classical symmetric velocity gradient tensor, perfectly matching the classical viscous stress tensor found in Newtonian Navier-Stokes equations.8 This ensures compatibility with the standard parabolic diffusion models inherently supported by FiniteVolumeMethod.jl.8

## **Formal Verification Framework and ASME Standards**

To formally quantify numerical uncertainty and verify the theoretical order of accuracy, the evaluation of the FiniteVolumeMethod.jl codebase must adhere to the ASME V\&V 20-2009 standard (Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Fluid Dynamics and Heat Transfer).2 This standard specifies a rigorous approach that uses concepts from experimental uncertainty analysis to consider errors and uncertainties in computational solutions.2  
The fundamental strategy of verification is to identify, quantify, and ultimately reduce errors in the computational model and its numerical solution.6 In this verification phase, the relationship of the simulation to the real physical world is irrelevant; the sole focus is on accurately coding and solving the mathematical equations as intended.4 Code verification assesses the reliability of the software coding and the implementation of numerical algorithms, typically by comparing outputs to classical analytical solutions or manufactured solutions.20 Solution verification, meanwhile, addresses the numerical error estimation of the computational solution for a specified set of conditions, focusing heavily on discretization errors.20

### **Grid Convergence Index (GCI) Evaluation**

The ASME V\&V 20-2009 standard dictates the use of the Grid Convergence Index (GCI), which is based on generalized Richardson Extrapolation, to report spatial and temporal discretization errors.9 The standard outlines a five-step procedure to reliably estimate these numerical uncertainties.23  
First, a representative grid size ![][image28] must be established for the unstructured or curvilinear meshes generated by FiniteVolumeMethod.jl.23 Second, the benchmark simulation must be executed on at least three significantly different grid resolutions (e.g., a coarse mesh ![][image29], a medium mesh ![][image30], and a fine mesh ![][image31]).9 The standard recommends that the grid refinement ratio ![][image32] should be strictly greater than ![][image33] to effectively separate the discretization error from standard numerical noise.9  
Third, the apparent order of accuracy ![][image34] of the numerical scheme must be calculated using the solutions obtained on the three grids.9 Assuming a constant refinement ratio ![][image35], the apparent order is evaluated as:  
![][image36]  
where ![][image37] represents the numerical solution of a specific state variable (e.g., density or velocity) on grid ![][image38].9  
Fourth, the extrapolated value of the solution ![][image39] is calculated, representing an estimate of the solution at a hypothetical grid spacing of zero.9 Finally, the Fine Grid Convergence Index is calculated.9 The GCI utilizes a factor of safety (![][image40]), which the ASME standard sets to ![][image41] when comparisons are made over three or more grids in the asymptotic convergence range.9 The index is given by:  
![][image42]  
For the FiniteVolumeMethod.jl package, which utilizes various flux limiters like minmod or superbee within its limiters.jl module to maintain Total Variation Diminishing (TVD) properties, the solver is theoretically expected to demonstrate an order of accuracy ![][image43] in smooth, continuous regions of the flow. However, the fundamental nature of TVD limiters forces the scheme to degrade to ![][image44] in the immediate vicinity of local extrema and shock waves to prevent unphysical oscillations.25 Demonstrating this exact degradation profile—second-order in smooth flows and first-order at discontinuities—is a definitive mathematical proof of correct limiter implementation.25

## **Algorithmic Verification via the Method of Manufactured Solutions**

Before comparing the code against complex physical phenomena or attempting validation against empirical data, the fundamental mathematical correctness of the spatial discretization, the numerical fluxes, and the highly complex geometric source term integration must be established.27 The premier technique for achieving this is the Method of Manufactured Solutions (MMS).27 MMS is a mathematically rigorous, gold-standard technique that determines if the code definitively achieves its theoretical order of accuracy across all implemented operators.29

### **MMS Formulation and Source Term Generation**

In the Method of Manufactured Solutions, an arbitrary, highly continuous analytical function ![][image45] is chosen a priori as the exact solution for the field variables.28 A major strength of the MMS procedure is that this chosen function does not need to represent a physically realistic scenario; the numerical code itself makes no distinction between "real" fluid dynamics and artificial mathematical constructs.31 The only requirement is that the manufactured solution must be sufficiently differentiable and complex enough to exercise all terms in the governing partial differential equations.27  
The differential operator ![][image46] of the numerical model is applied analytically to this manufactured solution.27 Because the chosen solution ![][image47] does not naturally satisfy the unforced governing equations, applying the operator yields a non-zero analytical residual.27 This residual is then explicitly added back into the computer code as a forcing function or external source term ![][image48].28 The modified equation solved by the code is therefore ![][image49].28  
For the Valencia formulation of GRMHD, the manufactured solution approach is particularly invaluable for verifying the highly non-linear geometric source terms.8 These terms involve complex tensor contractions, Christoffel symbols, and spatial derivatives of the metric tensor.8 The modified system for MMS testing becomes:  
![][image50]  
Because manual derivation of ![][image51] for the full 3+1 GRMHD equations is highly prone to human error, the generation of these analytical source terms is typically automated using symbolic mathematics libraries, such as Python's SymPy, which can export the closed-form representations directly into the Julia testing suite.29

## **Foundational Hydrodynamic and Viscous Benchmarks**

Once MMS verifies that the differential operators and source term integrations are free of coding defects, the software must be evaluated against classical analytical and highly accurate numerical solutions in the purely hydrodynamic and viscous limits. This step proves that the complex Israel-Stewart relaxation schemes properly degrade to classical Navier-Stokes behaviors as intended.8

### **The Taylor-Green Vortex (Viscous Decay)**

The Taylor-Green vortex is an exact, closed-form solution to the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations that simulates the exponential decay of a two-dimensional vortex grid entirely due to viscous dissipation.32 In the context of a relativistic simulation software, this benchmark rigorously tests the coupling of the momentum conservation equations with the shear stress tensor in the non-relativistic, weak-gravity limit.

| Parameter | Configuration |
| :---- | :---- |
| Domain Bounds | ![][image63] |
| Boundary Conditions | Periodic on all sides |
| Initial Velocity (![][image64]) | ![][image65] |
| Initial Velocity (![][image66]) | ![][image67] |
| Initial Pressure (![][image68]) | ![][image69] |
| Reynolds Number (![][image70]) | ![][image71] |
| Exact Solution Evolution | ![][image72] |

By initializing FiniteVolumeMethod.jl with an extremely small relaxation time ![][image26] in its viscous formulation, the output must precisely trace the theoretical exponential decay of the total kinetic energy, ![][image73].33 Any deviations from this precise decay rate immediately indicate a failure in the calculation of numerical viscosity, excessive inherent numerical diffusion from the Riemann solver, or an outright error in the formulation of the Israel-Stewart shear tensor.34

### **Lid-Driven Cavity Flow**

The lid-driven cavity is a cornerstone verification case used to study the fundamental aspects of incompressible flows in confined volumes.35 The geometry consists of a square container where the top boundary wall translates tangentially at a constant velocity, driving fluid motion strictly through viscous shear forces.36  
The models.jl implementations for 2D advection-diffusion must be tested across a range of Reynolds numbers (from ![][image74] up to ![][image75]).15 At lower Reynolds numbers, the code must accurately resolve the primary central vortex.35 As the Reynolds number increases beyond ![][image76], the simulation must reliably capture the emergence and growth of secondary vortices in the bottom corners of the cavity without these features numerically merging into the primary flow.35 The precise locations of the vortex centers and their corresponding vorticity magnitudes must be compared against standard literature benchmarks to verify the spatial discretization of the boundary conditions.34

### **Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability**

To verify the code's ability to handle shear flows, multi-mode perturbations, and to assess the inherent numerical diffusion of the chosen shock-capturing schemes, the Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability (KHI) is utilized.37 This instability develops spontaneously at the interface between two fluids flowing with a common shear layer.37

| :---- | :---- |
| Domain Bounds | $ \\times \[-0.5, 0.5\]$ |
| Boundary Conditions | Periodic in X-direction, Outflow in Y-direction |
| Density Profile | ![][image77] for ![][image78], otherwise ![][image79] |
| Velocity Profile (![][image64]) | ![][image80] for ![][image78], otherwise ![][image81] |
| Pressure | ![][image82] uniform across domain |
| Adiabatic Index (![][image83]) | ![][image84] |
| Initial Perturbation | Random noise ![][image85] added to interface |

The initial discontinuity acts as a slip surface.39 The metric of success is the accurate measurement of the growth rate of transverse kinetic energy during the linear phase, and the qualitative topological structure of the "cat-eye" vortices during the non-linear saturation phase.38 This test is highly sensitive to the dissipation characteristics of the chosen Riemann solver.37 If the basic HLL solver is used, the cat-eye vortices will smear prematurely due to excess numerical diffusion.8 If higher-order reconstruction schemes or less diffusive solvers (such as HLLC or HLLD) are applied, the thin filamentary structures connecting the vortices must maintain sharp density gradients for significantly longer simulation times.40

## **Special Relativistic and Newtonian MHD Benchmarks**

Transitioning up the complexity hierarchy, the verification protocol must address the coupling of the fluid equations with Maxwell's equations through the ideal MHD limit.8 A non-negotiable requirement for any rigorous MHD code is the strict maintenance of the solenoidal constraint (![][image86]).8 The FiniteVolumeMethod.jl package's implementation of Constrained Transport (CT) is explicitly tested in this phase.8 The CT approach utilizes a highly specific staggered grid architecture where magnetic field components are strictly tracked on cell faces, and electric fields (electromotive forces) are evaluated on cell edges.8

### **Brio-Wu MHD Shock Tube**

The Brio-Wu shock tube is the canonical 1D Riemann problem for magnetohydrodynamics, serving as the direct magnetic counterpart to the purely hydrodynamic Sod shock tube.25 It is the definitive test of an MHD solver's ability to accurately resolve the complex, overlapping wave structures unique to magnetized plasmas: fast and slow shocks, rarefaction waves, contact discontinuities, and compound structures.45

| Parameter | Left State (x\<0.5) | Right State (x\>0.5) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Density (![][image21]) | ![][image87] | ![][image88] |
| Velocity (![][image89]) | ![][image90] | ![][image90] |
| Pressure (![][image68]) | ![][image87] | ![][image91] |
| Transverse B-field (![][image92]) | ![][image87] | ![][image93] |
| **Global Parameters** | **![][image94]** (Uniform), ![][image95] | Domain length: ![][image87] |

The presence of the constant longitudinal magnetic field (![][image94]) fundamentally couples the transverse and longitudinal momentum equations.25 While an exact closed-form analytical solution does not exist for the Brio-Wu problem due to the non-linear complexity of the MHD equations, high-resolution numerical reference solutions are universally accepted as the gold standard for verification.25  
The solver must accurately capture five distinct wave structures propagating outward from the initial discontinuity at ![][image96].25 Moving from left to right, the code must resolve: a fast rarefaction wave, a slow compound wave, a contact discontinuity, a slow shock, and a fast rarefaction wave.45 This test serves to definitively distinguish the capabilities of different approximate Riemann solvers.41 If FiniteVolumeMethod.jl utilizes the simple HLL Riemann solver, the central contact discontinuity will be severely diffused.8 This occurs because the HLL solver inherently assumes a wave structure consisting of only two outermost waves separating the left and right states, lumping all intermediate structures (including Alfvén waves and contact discontinuities) into a single, highly diffusive intermediate state.8  
Replacing HLL with the HLLD solver—a sophisticated high-fidelity five-wave model that explicitly resolves intermediate Alfvénic and contact modes—must yield significantly sharper discontinuities in both the density and transverse magnetic field profiles.8 The validation suite must execute the shock tube using both solvers and programmatically verify that the ![][image58] error norm of the HLLD density profile is strictly lower than that of the HLL profile, confirming the successful implementation of the multi-state solver.42

### **Orszag-Tang MHD Vortex**

The Orszag-Tang vortex is an essential 2D benchmark that tracks the transition of a smooth, deterministic initial state into fully developed supersonic MHD turbulence.25 It rigorously tests the robustness of the flux limiters, the Riemann solver's handling of shock-shock interactions, and, most critically, the Constrained Transport divergence-cleaning mechanisms.43

| :---- | :---- |
| Domain Bounds | ![][image63] |
| Boundary Conditions | Periodic on all boundaries |
| Initial Velocity Field | ![][image97] |
| Initial Magnetic Field | ![][image98] |
| Fluid Density (![][image21]) | ![][image99] |
| Fluid Pressure (![][image68]) | ![][image100] |
| Adiabatic Index (![][image83]) | ![][image101] |

The initial magnetic field is constructed by taking the curl of a predefined vector potential ![][image102] evaluated at the zone corners.48 This guarantees that the initial state is analytically divergence-free (![][image103]).48 As the simulation evolves toward ![][image104], the initial large-scale vortices interact, driving the formation of complex current sheets and sharp MHD shocks.25  
The primary quantitative verification metric for this test is not just the flow morphology, but the strict programmatic monitoring of the maximum magnetic divergence ![][image105] over the entire computational grid at every time step.43 If the Constrained Transport (CT) algorithm in FiniteVolumeMethod.jl is implemented correctly on the staggered mesh, the divergence of the magnetic field must remain bounded strictly at machine precision (![][image106]), irrespective of the spatial resolution employed or the severity of the turbulent shocks generated.8 An accumulation of divergence errors would induce spurious magnetic monopoles, leading to artificial forces parallel to the magnetic field lines and an eventual catastrophic breakdown of the simulation.43

## **General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) Benchmarks**

At the absolute apex of the physical hierarchy, the software must be tested against solutions that involve strong spacetime curvature, ultra-relativistic fluid velocities, and deep gravitational potentials. The proper numerical evaluation of the geometric source terms ![][image8] and the stability of the Con2Prim (Conserved-to-Primitive) inversion algorithms are the central focus of these relativistic tests.8

### **Relativistic Linear Wave Convergence**

Before subjecting the GRMHD module to highly non-linear flows and black hole spacetimes, it must pass a comprehensive linear wave convergence test.50 This assesses the accuracy and fundamental correctness of the algorithm in the linear regime where wave dynamics can be treated entirely analytically.50  
Extremely small amplitude perturbations (![][image107]) are injected into a uniform background state moving with a highly relativistic bulk velocity. The perturbations must correspond exactly to the characteristic eigenmodes of the GRMHD system: the entropy waves, the fast and slow magnetosonic waves, and the Alfvén waves.11  
The wave is allowed to propagate across a periodic domain for exactly one full wavelength. The numerical error is then calculated as ![][image108] across the entire grid.50 For the second-order spatial reconstruction schemes provided in FiniteVolumeMethod.jl, the discretization error must scale precisely as ![][image109] as the grid is refined.50 Any deviation from pristine second-order convergence indicates a subtle flaw in the flux interpolation, the source term coupling, or the temporal integration interface (such as the linkage with the SciML ODE solvers via sciml\_bridge.jl).

### **Magnetized Bondi and Michel Spherical Accretion**

Bondi accretion describes the steady, spherically symmetric, transonic inflow of matter onto a massive central object.52 The classical Newtonian Bondi solution is generalized to Schwarzschild spacetime by the Michel solution.52 This problem is exceptionally critical for verifying the implementation of the static Schwarzschild metric, the handling of spherical coordinate singularities, and the correct integration of the radial geometric source terms.52

| Parameter | Configuration |
| :---- | :---- |
| Spacetime Metric | Schwarzschild Black Hole (Spin ![][image110]) |
| Inner Boundary | Inside the Event Horizon (![][image111]) |
| Outer Boundary | ![][image112] |
| Sonic Point | ![][image113] |
| Adiabatic Index (![][image83]) | ![][image114] |

The Michel solution provides an exact, semi-analytic profile for density, internal energy, and radial velocity.54 The FVM solver must maintain this initial steady state indefinitely without drifting.55 The mass accretion rate ![][image115] must remain constant across all radii to machine precision, directly verifying the continuity equation in heavily curved spacetime.52  
When a dynamically weak radial magnetic field (a magnetic monopole configuration, permitted locally purely for testing purposes) is introduced, the system transitions to Magnetized Bondi Accretion.56 If the magnetic field strength is increased to ![][image116] (where plasma beta ![][image117]), the immense magnetic pressure begins to significantly decelerate the radial infall of the plasma.57 The accretion rate ![][image118] drops drastically compared to the pure hydrodynamic Bondi rate ![][image119], often by over two orders of magnitude.57 The code must successfully replicate this magnetic suppression of the accretion rate without the Con2Prim routine crashing in the highly magnetized, low-density regions near the event horizon.16

### **The Fishbone-Moncrief Torus**

The ultimate verification and validation case for a GRMHD code aimed at advanced astrophysical applications is the Fishbone-Moncrief torus.60 It represents a thick, rotationally supported accretion disk in perfect hydrostatic equilibrium around a rapidly spinning Kerr black hole.62

| Parameter | Configuration |
| :---- | :---- |
| Spacetime Metric | Kerr Black Hole, Spin Parameter ![][image120] 64 |
| Disk Inner Edge | ![][image121] or ![][image122] 61 |
| Pressure Maximum | ![][image123] or ![][image124] 61 |
| Adiabatic Index (![][image83]) | ![][image114] or ![][image101] 62 |
| Magnetic Vector Potential | ![][image125] 64 |

The testing of this configuration proceeds in three distinct phases:

1. **Stationary Equilibrium Check**: First, the simulation must be executed purely hydrodynamically, with no magnetic fields present. Because the analytical Fishbone-Moncrief solution exactly balances the Kerr spacetime gravitational forces, the centrifugal force, and the fluid pressure gradients, the torus must remain completely stationary.62 Any evolution in the velocity field or shifting of the density contours (beyond truncation-level grid noise) immediately exposes errors in the spatial discretization of the metric tensor derivatives ![][image126] within the geometric source terms ![][image8].8  
2. **Magnetorotational Instability (MRI) Evolution**: Second, a weak poloidal magnetic field loop is seeded within the interior of the torus using the vector potential ![][image127].64 The differential rotation of the accretion disk rapidly stretches and shears these magnetic field lines, triggering the Magnetorotational Instability (MRI).57 The verification metric shifts from maintaining stationarity to accurately resolving turbulence. The code must demonstrate the exponential growth of the magnetic energy during the linear phase and eventually reach a saturated, highly turbulent state that drives accretion inward across the event horizon while launching a Poynting-flux dominated jet along the black hole's spin axis.64  
3. **Con2Prim Robustness in Vacuum**: As the relativistic jet evacuates the polar regions along the spin axis, the rest-mass density ![][image21] approaches absolute zero while the magnetic field energy ![][image128] remains extremely high, creating an extreme magnetic-to-fluid pressure ratio (![][image129]).16 This vacuum-like, highly magnetized state severely stresses the Newton-Raphson iteration in the Con2Prim variable recovery scheme, which struggles to find real roots for the Lorentz factor.8 A robust, production-ready software product must flawlessly fall back to specialized robust solvers (e.g., 1D or 2D entropy-based recovery methods) or dynamically apply density "floors" rather than returning non-physical negative densities or NaNs, ensuring the simulation runs uninterrupted for thousands of gravitational times (![][image130]).16

## **Infrastructure Validation and Quality Assurance**

Beyond solving the partial differential equations, the overarching architecture of the FiniteVolumeMethod.jl software must be rigorously validated against modern software engineering standards and CI/CD (Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment) protocols.21

### **Integration with SciML and Temporal Verification**

The Julia package utilizes sciml\_bridge.jl to cast the assembled FVM spatial discretizations into standard ODEProblem objects, elegantly delegating the time integration to the broader SciML ecosystem. Verification must ensure that the carefully established spatial order of accuracy is not polluted by temporal truncation errors. This is achieved by running the aforementioned benchmarks using explicit Runge-Kutta methods of varying temporal orders (e.g., RK2, RK4, SSPRK3). The time-step ![][image131] must be tightly constrained by the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition, which, in the highly dynamic GRMHD regime, must account for the speed of light in curved spacetime by actively calculating the fastest fast-magnetosonic wave speeds at every cell interface.11

### **Repository Governance and Continuous Integration**

To guarantee that the codebase remains continuously verified throughout its development lifecycle, the testing suite documented in scientific\_evidence.jl acts as a highly automated regression framework.  
The integration of a validation/manifest.toml strictly version-controls the exact physical parameters, grid resolutions, and expected error bounds of every benchmark discussed in this report. By programmatically executing quality\_ledger.jl and repository\_governance.jl, the software's CI pipeline actively verifies that future modifications to critical components—such as the high-resolution flux limiters in limiters.jl or the complex geometric mapping routines in curvilinear.jl—do not violate the verified error norms. Specifically, the automated tests must assert that the exact ![][image58] and ![][image60] norms computed via the ASME V\&V 20-2009 GCI procedure remain stable, ensuring that no performance optimizations silently degrade the physical accuracy of the solver.2

## **Conclusion**

The exhaustive verification of a Finite Volume Method software suite designed for General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics is a monumental computational physics challenge. It requires a mathematically rigorous journey from the deepest abstractions of curved spacetime geometry down to the classical, everyday behaviors of Newtonian viscous fluids.  
By systematically employing the Method of Manufactured Solutions, the fundamental calculus of the software's spatial operators and source term integrators is mathematically proven beyond reproach. By executing the Taylor-Green vortex and Kelvin-Helmholtz instability tests, the asymptotic reduction to Navier-Stokes limits and the careful mitigation of numerical diffusion are validated. By deploying the Brio-Wu shock tube and Orszag-Tang vortex tests, the necessity of advanced Riemann solvers like HLLD and the absolute requirement of Constrained Transport for maintaining ![][image86] are confirmed. Finally, by successfully stabilizing the Michel-Bondi spherical accretion flow and accurately resolving the MRI-driven turbulence of the Fishbone-Moncrief torus, the software proves its advanced capability to handle extreme gravity, ultra-relativistic speeds, and highly magnetized vacuum states.  
When these exacting benchmarks are codified directly into the scientific\_evidence.jl manifest and constantly evaluated against the stringent metrics of the ASME V\&V 20-2009 standards, the FiniteVolumeMethod.jl package transcends being merely an academic research code. It establishes itself as a mathematically verified, production-grade computational instrument, fully capable of providing high-fidelity predictive capability for the most extreme and dynamic environments in the universe.
